To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
vitamin C is a micronutrient with a key role in the immune system.

(i) the role of vitamin C as a supplement for the general population is still unclear, although it is well known to have an important role in immune function; (ii) vitamin C supplementation may be useful in subjects with low vitamin C plasma concentration; (iii) vitamin C infusion may be a useful tool to reduce inflammation and to improve immune response in critically ill patients; (iv) vitamin C infusion is currently under evaluation in COVID 19 patients.
vitamin C supplementation is not effective in reducing the risk of developing respiratory tract infections and that it may have beneficial effects in critically ill COVID 19 patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the potential of vitamin C as a therapeutic agent for the prevention and/or treatment of respiratory diseases, including COVID 19, and with the possible role of vitamin C in the modulation of the immune system.
the role of vitamin C in the immune system, with particular reference to the prevention and treatment, both in the acute and in the critical phase, of the COVID 19 infection.

the role of vitamin C in the treatment of acute respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia and influenza, and the possible application of vitamin C supplementation in the treatment of COVID 19.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence supporting the use of vitamin supplementation in the prevention and treatment COVID 19 is still lacking.
the use of vitamin c supplements in the prevention of respiratory infections is not justified.

vitamin C is an essential micronutrient, with a key role in maintaining the immune function and preventing respiratory diseases, but that its supplementation in the general population does not seem to be justified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
vitamin C supplementation is not recommended in the general population to prevent or treat respiratory infections, including COVID-19, unless there is a clear indication for it.

, although vitamin C supplementation may not be effective in preventing or treating the common cold, it can play a key role in the prevention and treatment in the most severe conditions of respiratory infections, such as the COVID-19 pneumonia.

vitamin C is a safe, cheap and widely available supplement with a potential role in the prevention and treatment in specific subgroups, such as the elderly or patients with low plasma levels of vitamin C, as well as in critically ill patients, but not for the general population.
The main takeaway from our work is that

vitamin C is not a cure for COVID 19 and its use should be limited to the treatment of patients with critical illness, while in healthy subjects its supplementation should not be considered a prophylactic measure.
the role of vitamin C in the prevention and treatment against COVID 19 is not yet clear and that further studies are needed to clarify its potential application during the current pandemic.

vitamin C has an important role in the modulation of the inflammatory response, but its potential role as a preventive and/or therapeutic agent in COVID 19 patients is still to be clarified and requires further investigation.
